questions.prompt: A 7B model you like needs more memory than your laptop has. Which lever first?
options: Fine-tune it on your data so it gets smaller
Quantize it to a lower precision
Distill it from a larger model
Nothing helps; you need a different model
questions.explanation: Quantization stores the same weights at lower precision, which is exactly a size and memory problem. Fine-tuning is the tempting answer because it is the most talked-about lever, but it does not change size at all, and distilling would make a *new* model rather than shrink this one.

questions.prompt: You have a large model doing a narrow classification task in production and want a cheap, small model that behaves the same on that task. Which lever?
options: Distill the large model's outputs into a small student
questions.explanation: Distillation trains a small student to imitate the large teacher on the inputs you cover, which is the definition of a cheap stand-in on a narrow task. Fine-tuning a frontier model is impossible anyway — you do not have its weights — and effort does not change size or cost the way this task needs.

questions.prompt: The model must follow your company's naming rules and never invent a part number. Which lever, and what must accompany it?
options: Quantize it; smaller models invent less
Fine-tune it on your data, with a held-out check set scored before and after
Distill it from a bigger model, with no measurement
Raise the effort level to maximum
questions.explanation: Teaching the model your domain is fine-tuning, and because it learns whatever is in your data — including your mistakes — it needs a held-out check set measured before and after. 'Smaller models invent less' is tempting folklore; quantization changes precision, not knowledge.

questions.prompt: After a fine-tune, the model sounds right more often but is wrong on edge cases it used to flag. What is the most likely cause?
options: The quantization got worse during training
Your training data encoded the errors, and there was no check set to catch the drift
You raised the effort level too far
The model is now too small
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning learns the behaviour in your data, wrong answers included, so it can make a wrong answer sound fluent. Without a held-out check set scored before and after, that drift is invisible until it ships.
